subject: Physics
question: a. Convert 2.5 gmm⁻² to kgm⁻².
modelAnswer:
1 g = 10⁻³ kg and 1 mm = 10⁻³ m, so 1 mm² = (10⁻³ m)² = 10⁻⁶ m².

2.5 g mm⁻² = (2.5 × 10⁻³ kg)/(10⁻⁶ m²)
= 2.5 × 10⁻³⁺⁶ kg m⁻²
= 2.5 × 10³ kg m⁻² (2500 kg m⁻²).

subject: Physics
question: b, Determine if the formula T = 2π√(m/(F/x)) is dimensionally correct. Where T is time period, m is mass, F is force and x is distance.
modelAnswer:
A formula is dimensionally correct if both sides have the same dimensions. 2π is a pure number, so it has no dimensions.

Left side: [T] = T.

Right side:
[m] = M
[F] = MLT⁻² (force = mass × acceleration)
[x] = L
[F/x] = MLT⁻²/L = MT⁻²
[m/(F/x)] = M/(MT⁻²) = T²
√(T²) = T.

Both sides have dimension T, so the formula is dimensionally correct.

subject: Physics
question: a. State the conditions for two vectors to be equal. Give any four examples of the term “magnitude” as applied to vector and scalar quantities.
modelAnswer:
Conditions for two vectors to be equal:
1. They must have the same magnitude.
2. They must point in the same direction.
(They must also represent the same kind of physical quantity, in the same units.)

Magnitude is the size (numerical value with its unit) of a quantity. Scalars have magnitude only; vectors have magnitude and direction. Examples:
1. Mass of 5 kg (scalar): magnitude 5 kg.
2. Speed of 20 m s⁻¹ (scalar): magnitude 20 m s⁻¹.
3. Velocity of 20 m s⁻¹ due north (vector): magnitude 20 m s⁻¹.
4. Force of 10 N acting vertically downwards (vector): magnitude 10 N.
(Other acceptable examples: temperature, energy, time, displacement, acceleration, momentum.)

subject: Physics
question: b. Two vectors having equal magnitudes f make an angle θ with each other. Find the magnitude of the resultant.
modelAnswer:
By the parallelogram (cosine) rule, for two vectors P and Q at angle θ:
R² = P² + Q² + 2PQ cos θ.

With P = Q = f:
R² = f² + f² + 2f² cos θ = 2f²(1 + cos θ).

Using 1 + cos θ = 2cos²(θ/2):
R² = 4f² cos²(θ/2)
R = 2f cos(θ/2).

The resultant bisects the angle between the two vectors, making θ/2 with each.

subject: Physics
question: A particle of mass 40g executes a simple harmonic motion of amplitude 2.0 cm. If the time period is 0.20 s, find the total mechanical energy of the system.
modelAnswer:
m = 40 g = 0.040 kg, A = 2.0 cm = 0.020 m, T = 0.20 s.

Angular frequency: ω = 2π/T = 2π/0.20 = 10π rad s⁻¹ (≈ 31.4 rad s⁻¹).

Total mechanical energy in SHM: E = ½mω²A²
= ½ × 0.040 × (10π)² × (0.020)²
= 0.020 × 100π² × 4.0 × 10⁻⁴
= 8π² × 10⁻⁴ J
≈ 7.9 × 10⁻³ J.

subject: Physics
question: A load of 4.0 kg is suspended from a ceiling through a steel wire of radius 2.0 mm. Find the tensile stress developed in the wire at equilibrium.
modelAnswer:
At equilibrium the tension in the wire equals the weight of the load.
F = mg = 4.0 × 10 = 40 N (g = 10 m s⁻², from the constants given).

Cross-sectional area: A = πr² = π × (2.0 × 10⁻³)² = 4π × 10⁻⁶ m² ≈ 1.257 × 10⁻⁵ m².

Tensile stress = F/A = 40/(1.257 × 10⁻⁵)
≈ 3.2 × 10⁶ N m⁻² (Pa).

subject: Physics
question: a. What is a fluid? Give two examples.
modelAnswer:
A fluid is a substance that can flow and has no fixed shape; it takes the shape of its container because it cannot resist a shearing force. Both liquids and gases are fluids.

Examples: water and air (others: oil, mercury, oxygen gas).

subject: Physics
question: b. Define the terms adhesion and cohesion
modelAnswer:
Adhesion is the force of attraction between molecules of different substances (e.g., between water molecules and glass, which makes water wet glass).

Cohesion is the force of attraction between molecules of the same substance (e.g., between mercury molecules, which makes mercury form droplets).

subject: Physics
question: Consider the wave y = 5sin(x − 60t). In terms of π, Find the wave number, the frequency, wavelength and velocity of the wave.
modelAnswer:
Compare with the standard progressive wave y = A sin(kx − ωt) (SI units assumed):
A = 5, k = 1 rad m⁻¹, ω = 60 rad s⁻¹.

Wave number: k = 1 rad m⁻¹. (If wave number is defined as 1/λ instead, it is 1/(2π) m⁻¹.)

Frequency: f = ω/(2π) = 60/(2π) = 30/π Hz (≈ 9.55 Hz).

Wavelength: λ = 2π/k = 2π/1 = 2π m.

Velocity: v = ω/k = 60/1 = 60 m s⁻¹.
Check: v = fλ = (30/π) × 2π = 60 m s⁻¹.

subject: Physics
question: Define the term entropy. A Carnot engine working between 27 °C and 127 °C takes up 800J of heat from the reservoir in one cycle. Calculate the work done by the engine and efficiency of the engine.
modelAnswer:
Entropy is a measure of the degree of disorder (randomness) of a system. The change in entropy is the heat absorbed reversibly divided by the absolute temperature at which it is absorbed: ΔS = Q/T (unit J K⁻¹).

The 800 J is taken from the hot reservoir.
T₁ (hot) = 127 + 273 = 400 K; T₂ (cold) = 27 + 273 = 300 K.

Efficiency: η = 1 − T₂/T₁ = 1 − 300/400 = 0.25 = 25%.

Work done: W = ηQ₁ = 0.25 × 800 = 200 J.
(The remaining 600 J is rejected to the cold reservoir.)

subject: Physics
question: Calculate the energy radiated per second by a sphere (assumed to be a blackbody radiator) of radius 10 cm maintained at a constant temperature of 727°C.
modelAnswer:
Stefan–Boltzmann law: P = σAT⁴ (emissivity = 1 for a blackbody).

T = 727 + 273 = 1000 K, so T⁴ = 10¹² K⁴.
r = 10 cm = 0.10 m; A = 4πr² = 4π × 0.010 = 0.1257 m².
σ = 5.7 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴ (given).

P = 5.7 × 10⁻⁸ × 0.1257 × 10¹²
= 5.7 × 10⁴ × 0.1257
≈ 7.2 × 10³ W.

The sphere radiates about 7.2 × 10³ J every second.

subject: Physics
question: A particle of mass 20 g is projected vertically upwards with a speed of 10 ms⁻¹. Find the work done by the force of gravity during the time the particle goes up.
modelAnswer:
m = 20 g = 0.020 kg, u = 10 m s⁻¹, g = 10 m s⁻².

Maximum height: v² = u² − 2gh, with v = 0 at the top:
h = u²/(2g) = 100/20 = 5.0 m.

Gravity acts downwards while the particle moves upwards, so its work is negative:
W = −mgh = −0.020 × 10 × 5.0 = −1.0 J.

Check with the work–energy theorem: W = ΔKE = 0 − ½ × 0.020 × 10² = −1.0 J.

subject: Physics
question: A platinum resistance thermometer reads 0°C when its resistance is 80 Ω and 100°C when its resistance is 90Ω. Find the temperature at the platinum scale at which the resistance is 86Ω.
modelAnswer:
On the platinum resistance scale:
θ = (R_θ − R₀)/(R₁₀₀ − R₀) × 100°C.

R₀ = 80 Ω, R₁₀₀ = 90 Ω, R_θ = 86 Ω.

θ = (86 − 80)/(90 − 80) × 100
= 6/10 × 100
= 60°C.

subject: Physics
question:
a. (i) Distinguish between the terms “conservative force and nonconservative force”, give one example for each.
(ii). A simple pendulum of length l, and mass m oscillates through an angle θ. Derive the expressions for its potential energy.
(iii) Determine the potential energy of a simple pendulum of length 90 cm and mass 0.5 kg displaced at angle of 60°.
modelAnswer:
(i) A conservative force is one whose work done in moving a body between two points does not depend on the path taken; the work done around any closed path is zero, so mechanical energy is conserved. Example: gravitational force (also elastic spring force, electrostatic force).
A nonconservative force is one whose work done depends on the path taken; work around a closed path is not zero, and mechanical energy is lost (usually as heat). Example: friction (also air resistance, viscous drag).

(ii) Let the bob hang from point O. At the lowest point the bob is a distance l below O. When the string makes angle θ with the vertical, the bob is l cos θ below O.
Height risen: h = l − l cos θ = l(1 − cos θ).
Potential energy relative to the lowest point:
PE = mgh = mgl(1 − cos θ).
For small angles, 1 − cos θ ≈ θ²/2, so PE ≈ ½mglθ² (θ in radians).

(iii) l = 90 cm = 0.90 m, m = 0.5 kg, θ = 60°, g = 10 m s⁻².
PE = mgl(1 − cos 60°) = 0.5 × 10 × 0.90 × (1 − 0.5)
= 4.5 × 0.5
= 2.25 J.

subject: Physics
question:
b. (i).The heat (H) produced in a wire carrying an electric current depends on the current (I), the resistance (R) and the time (t). Assuming that, the dependence is related by the equation H α IˣRʸtᶻ. Use dimensional analysis to determine the values of the indices (x, y, z). Hence, find the expression for H.
(ii) A solid object has a mass (400.3 ± 0.02)g and volume (75.6 ± 0.01)cm³. Calculate the density of the solid with the associated error.
modelAnswer:
(i) Note: the paper prints α (alpha); it means ∝ (is proportional to).

H = kIˣRʸtᶻ, where k is a dimensionless constant.

Dimensions (A = ampere):
[H] = energy = ML²T⁻²
[I] = A
[R] = V/A = (energy per charge)/current = (ML²T⁻²/AT)/A = ML²T⁻³A⁻²
[t] = T

ML²T⁻² = Aˣ (ML²T⁻³A⁻²)ʸ Tᶻ = Mʸ L²ʸ T⁻³ʸ⁺ᶻ Aˣ⁻²ʸ

Equate powers:
M: y = 1
L: 2y = 2 → y = 1 (consistent)
A: x − 2y = 0 → x = 2
T: −3y + z = −2 → z = 1

x = 2, y = 1, z = 1, so H = kI²Rt. In SI units k = 1, giving H = I²Rt (Joule's law of heating).

(ii) Density: ρ = m/V = 400.3/75.6 = 5.295 g cm⁻³.

For a quotient, fractional errors add:
Δρ/ρ = Δm/m + ΔV/V = 0.02/400.3 + 0.01/75.6
= 0.0000500 + 0.000132
= 0.000182.

Δρ = 0.000182 × 5.295 = 0.00096 ≈ 0.001 g cm⁻³.

ρ = (5.295 ± 0.001) g cm⁻³ = (5295 ± 1) kg m⁻³.

subject: Physics
question:
a. (i). Explain the terms center of mass (CM) and center of gravity (CG). How do these related to the rigid body?
(ii) Three particles of masses 1.0 kg, 2.0 kg and 3.0 kg are placed at the corners A, B and C respectively of an equilateral triangle ABC of side 1 m as shown in figure 1. What is the center of mass of the system?

image.alt: Equilateral triangle ABC of side 1 m on x–y axes: B at the origin (0, 0), C on the x-axis labelled (1, 1), and A at the apex labelled (1/2, √3/2)

modelAnswer:
Figure 1: equilateral triangle ABC of side 1 m on x–y axes, with B at the origin (0, 0), C on the x-axis labelled (1, 1), and A at the apex labelled (1/2, √3/2).

(i) The centre of mass (CM) is the point at which the whole mass of a body or system of particles can be considered to be concentrated; it moves as if all external forces act on it.
The centre of gravity (CG) is the point through which the resultant weight (force of gravity) of the body acts.
Relation to a rigid body: in a rigid body the distances between particles are fixed, so the CM is a fixed point in the body (it may lie outside the material, e.g., in a ring). In a uniform gravitational field, such as near the earth's surface, the CG and CM of a rigid body coincide. They differ only if g varies across the body (e.g., a very tall structure).

(ii) Misprint note: Figure 1 labels C as (1, 1). Since B is at (0, 0), BC = 1 m lies along the x-axis, so C must be (1, 0). (1, 0) is used below.

A (1.0 kg) at (0.5, √3/2), B (2.0 kg) at (0, 0), C (3.0 kg) at (1, 0). Total mass M = 6.0 kg.

x_cm = Σmx/M = (1.0 × 0.5 + 2.0 × 0 + 3.0 × 1)/6.0 = 3.5/6.0 = 7/12 m ≈ 0.583 m.

y_cm = Σmy/M = (1.0 × √3/2 + 2.0 × 0 + 3.0 × 0)/6.0 = (√3/2)/6.0 = √3/12 m ≈ 0.144 m.

Centre of mass: (7/12, √3/12) m ≈ (0.583 m, 0.144 m), measured from B.

subject: Physics
question:
b(i). Two particles of masses 1 kg and 2 kg are placed at a separation of 50 cm. Calculate the force acting between them. Assuming that the only force acting on the particles are their mutual gravitation, find the initial accelerations of the each particle.
(ii). Calculate the escape velocity from the moon. The mass of the moon = 7.4 x 10²² kg and radius of the moon = 1740 km.
modelAnswer:
(i) Newton's law of gravitation: F = Gm₁m₂/r².
m₁ = 1 kg, m₂ = 2 kg, r = 50 cm = 0.50 m, G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻².

F = (6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 1 × 2)/(0.50)²
= (1.334 × 10⁻¹⁰)/0.25
= 5.34 × 10⁻¹⁰ N (attractive).

The same force acts on each particle (Newton's third law), so a = F/m:
Acceleration of the 1 kg particle: a₁ = 5.34 × 10⁻¹⁰/1 = 5.34 × 10⁻¹⁰ m s⁻².
Acceleration of the 2 kg particle: a₂ = 5.34 × 10⁻¹⁰/2 = 2.67 × 10⁻¹⁰ m s⁻².
Both accelerations are directed towards the other particle.

(ii) Escape velocity: v_e = √(2GM/R).
M = 7.4 × 10²² kg, R = 1740 km = 1.74 × 10⁶ m.

2GM = 2 × 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 7.4 × 10²² = 9.87 × 10¹²
2GM/R = 9.87 × 10¹²/1.74 × 10⁶ = 5.67 × 10⁶ m² s⁻²
v_e = √(5.67 × 10⁶) ≈ 2.38 × 10³ m s⁻¹ (about 2.4 km s⁻¹).

subject: Physics
question:
a.(i) Define the terms viscosity and coefficient of viscosity. State the SI unit and dimensions of coefficient of viscosity.
(ii). Write the mathematical expression for Stokes’s law and state the meaning of each symbol.
(iii). Consider a metallic sphere of radius ‘a’ and density ρ to fall under gravity in a liquid of density σ. Sketch the forces acting on the sphere. Hence, Show that the terminal velocity is given by v = 2a²(ρ − σ)g/(9η).
modelAnswer:
(i) Viscosity is the internal friction in a fluid that opposes the relative motion between its adjacent layers.
The coefficient of viscosity (η) is the tangential force per unit area needed to maintain a unit velocity gradient between layers of the fluid:
η = F/(A × dv/dx).
SI unit: N s m⁻² (equivalently Pa s, or kg m⁻¹ s⁻¹).
Dimensions: [F]/([A][dv/dx]) = MLT⁻²/(L² × T⁻¹) = ML⁻¹T⁻¹.

Misprint note: the list of constants gives the viscosity of water at 10°C as 1.3 × 10⁹ N m⁻² s. The correct value is about 1.3 × 10⁻³ N s m⁻².

(ii) Stokes's law: F = 6πηav (often written F = 6πηrv)
F = viscous (drag) force on the sphere
η = coefficient of viscosity of the fluid
a (or r) = radius of the sphere
v = velocity of the sphere through the fluid.

(iii) Sketch: draw the sphere with three arrows: its weight W acting downwards, and the upthrust U and viscous drag F both acting upwards.

Weight: W = (4/3)πa³ρg
Upthrust (weight of liquid displaced): U = (4/3)πa³σg
Viscous drag: F = 6πηav

As the sphere speeds up, the drag increases until the net force is zero. The sphere then moves at its terminal velocity v:
W = U + F
(4/3)πa³ρg = (4/3)πa³σg + 6πηav
6πηav = (4/3)πa³(ρ − σ)g
v = (4/3)πa³(ρ − σ)g/(6πηa)
v = 2a²(ρ − σ)g/(9η), as required.

subject: Physics
question:
b(i).State two conditions for liquid to be ideal.
(ii). A liquid of mass m and volume V is flowing with velocity v, derive the expressions for its kinetic and potential energies per unit volume of the liquid in terms of ρ.
modelAnswer:
(i) Conditions for an ideal liquid (any two):
1. It is incompressible (its density is constant).
2. It is non-viscous (no internal friction).
3. Its flow is steady (streamline): the velocity at any point does not change with time.
4. Its flow is irrotational.

(ii) Density: ρ = m/V.

Kinetic energy per unit volume:
KE = ½mv², so KE/V = ½(m/V)v² = ½ρv².

Potential energy per unit volume: the question gives no height, so let the liquid be at height h above a reference level.
PE = mgh, so PE/V = (m/V)gh = ρgh.

(These are the ½ρv² and ρgh terms of Bernoulli's equation: P + ½ρv² + ρgh = constant.)

subject: Physics
question:
a(i). State the zeroth and first laws of thermodynamics.
(ii). An 0.050 kg block of Aluminum is heated and placed in a calorimeter containing 0.10 kg of water at 20°C. If the final temperature of the water was 30°C, to what temperature was the Aluminum heated? (Specific heat capacity of Aluminum is 900 Jkg⁻¹K⁻¹).
modelAnswer:
(i) Zeroth law: if two systems are each in thermal equilibrium with a third system, then they are in thermal equilibrium with each other. (This is the basis of temperature measurement.)
First law: the heat supplied to a system equals the increase in its internal energy plus the external work done by the system: ΔQ = ΔU + ΔW. (It is a statement of conservation of energy.)

(ii) The heat capacity of the calorimeter is not given, so it is neglected. Heat lost by aluminium = heat gained by water.

Heat gained by water = m_w c_w Δθ = 0.10 × 4200 × (30 − 20) = 4200 J.

Let the initial temperature of the aluminium be T.
Heat lost by aluminium = 0.050 × 900 × (T − 30) = 45(T − 30).

45(T − 30) = 4200
T − 30 = 93.3
T ≈ 123°C.

subject: Physics
question:
b. (i). State and briefly explain the three phases of matter with respect to atomic view. What causes the phase changes in matter?
(ii). How much heat is required to raise the temperature of 0.015 kg of water from −25.0°C to 125.0°C?
modelAnswer:
(i) Solid: atoms/molecules are closely packed in fixed positions and only vibrate about these positions; strong intermolecular forces give a definite shape and volume.
Liquid: molecules are close together but can move past one another; intermolecular forces are weaker, so a liquid has a definite volume but takes the shape of its container.
Gas: molecules are far apart and move randomly at high speeds; intermolecular forces are negligible, so a gas has no definite shape or volume and fills its container.

Cause of phase changes: adding or removing heat energy (or changing the pressure). Supplying heat increases the kinetic energy of the particles until they overcome the intermolecular forces holding them together (melting, boiling). Removing heat lets the forces pull them back together (condensation, freezing). During a phase change the temperature stays constant; the energy involved is the latent heat.

(ii) Note: at −25.0°C the water is ice, and at 125.0°C it is steam. The paper gives only c_w = 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ and L_v = 2.2 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹. The following standard values are assumed: specific heat capacity of ice = 2100 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹, latent heat of fusion of ice = 3.34 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹, and specific heat capacity of steam = 2010 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. Different assumed values will change the final answer slightly.

m = 0.015 kg.
1. Ice from −25°C to 0°C: 0.015 × 2100 × 25 = 787.5 J
2. Melting ice at 0°C: 0.015 × 3.34 × 10⁵ = 5010 J
3. Water from 0°C to 100°C: 0.015 × 4200 × 100 = 6300 J
4. Boiling water at 100°C: 0.015 × 2.2 × 10⁶ = 33 000 J
5. Steam from 100°C to 125°C: 0.015 × 2010 × 25 = 753.75 J

Total = 787.5 + 5010 + 6300 + 33 000 + 753.75 = 45 851 J ≈ 4.6 × 10⁴ J.

subject: Physics
question:
a(i). Distinguish between the terms Heat transfer and thermal conductivity.
(ii). State and explain all the mechanisms of heat transfer.
(iii). A piece of brass is 5.0 mm thick and has a cross-sectional area of 0.010 m². If the temperature on one side of the metal is 65°C and the temperature on the other side is 25°C, how much heat will be conducted through the metal in 30 s? The coefficient of thermal conductivity for brass is 120WK⁻¹m⁻².
modelAnswer:
(i) Heat transfer is the flow of thermal energy from a region of higher temperature to a region of lower temperature.
Thermal conductivity (k) is a property of a material: the rate of heat flow per unit area per unit temperature gradient through it, k = (Q/t)/(A × Δθ/x). It measures how well the material conducts heat. Unit: W m⁻¹ K⁻¹.

(ii) Mechanisms of heat transfer:
1. Conduction: heat passes through a material from particle to particle by vibrations (and, in metals, by free electrons), without the material itself moving. It is the main mode in solids.
2. Convection: heat is carried by the actual movement of a fluid. Heated fluid expands, becomes less dense and rises, and cooler, denser fluid sinks to take its place, setting up convection currents. It occurs in liquids and gases.
3. Radiation: heat is transferred as electromagnetic (mainly infrared) waves. It needs no medium, so it can cross a vacuum (e.g., heat from the sun).

(iii) Misprint note: the paper gives the unit as W K⁻¹ m⁻². The correct unit of thermal conductivity is W m⁻¹ K⁻¹.

Q = kAΔθt/x
k = 120 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹, A = 0.010 m², Δθ = 65 − 25 = 40 K, x = 5.0 mm = 5.0 × 10⁻³ m, t = 30 s.

Rate of heat flow: Q/t = (120 × 0.010 × 40)/(5.0 × 10⁻³) = 48/0.005 = 9600 W.
Heat conducted in 30 s: Q = 9600 × 30 = 2.88 × 10⁵ J.

subject: Physics
question:
b. When a metallic bar is heated from 0°C to 100°C, its length increases by 0.05%. Obtain
(i) The coefficient of linear expansion of the metal.
(ii) The percentage increase of the volume of the bar.
modelAnswer:
(i) ΔL/L₀ = 0.05% = 0.05/100 = 5.0 × 10⁻⁴; Δθ = 100 K.

α = ΔL/(L₀Δθ) = 5.0 × 10⁻⁴/100 = 5.0 × 10⁻⁶ K⁻¹.

(ii) Coefficient of cubic expansion: γ = 3α = 1.5 × 10⁻⁵ K⁻¹.
ΔV/V₀ = γΔθ = 1.5 × 10⁻⁵ × 100 = 1.5 × 10⁻³.
Percentage increase in volume = 1.5 × 10⁻³ × 100% = 0.15%.
(This is three times the percentage increase in length.)

subject: Physics
question:
a (i) State the quantity that remains constant for each of the following thermodynamic processes.
(A) Isobaric process B).Isochoric process C) Isothermal process D) Adiabatic process.
(ii) Show that, for a monatomic ideal gas undergoing an adiabatic process, PV^(5/3) = constant.
modelAnswer:
(i)
(A) Isobaric process: pressure is constant.
(B) Isochoric process: volume is constant.
(C) Isothermal process: temperature is constant (so the internal energy of an ideal gas is constant).
(D) Adiabatic process: heat content is constant; no heat enters or leaves the system (ΔQ = 0). For a reversible adiabatic process, entropy is also constant.

(ii) Consider n moles of ideal gas.
Adiabatic: dQ = 0, so by the first law dU + P dV = 0.
For an ideal gas dU = nC_v dT, so nC_v dT = −P dV. ...(1)

From PV = nRT: P dV + V dP = nR dT. ...(2)

Substitute nR dT = (R/C_v)(nC_v dT) = −(R/C_v)P dV into (2):
P dV + V dP = −(R/C_v)P dV
V dP + (1 + R/C_v)P dV = 0.

Since C_p = C_v + R, we have 1 + R/C_v = C_p/C_v = γ:
V dP + γP dV = 0
dP/P + γ dV/V = 0.

Integrating: ln P + γ ln V = constant, so PV^γ = constant.

For a monatomic ideal gas, C_v = (3/2)R and C_p = (5/2)R, so γ = 5/3.
Hence PV^(5/3) = constant.

subject: Physics
question:
b(i) Write down ( without proof) the efficiency for a Carnot cycle as a function of the:
A) Heat that flows to and from the reservoirs and
B) Temperatures of the two reservoirs.
(ii) A wire 10 m long and cross sectional area of 20 mm² is stretched 2,5cm by a 20 kg lead block when attached to it, find:
(A). The tensile stress (B) tensile strain (C) Young modulus of the wire.
(iii) The internal energy of a gas is given by U = 1.5pV. It expands from 100cm³ to 200cm³ against a constant pressure of 1.0 x 10⁵ Pa. Calculate the heat absorbed by the gas in the process.
modelAnswer:
(i)
(A) η = 1 − Q₂/Q₁, where Q₁ = heat absorbed from the hot reservoir and Q₂ = heat rejected to the cold reservoir.
(B) η = 1 − T₂/T₁, where T₁ and T₂ are the absolute temperatures (in K) of the hot and cold reservoirs.

(ii) Misprint note: the paper prints the extension as 2,5cm; this is taken as 2.5 cm.

F = mg = 20 × 10 = 200 N; A = 20 mm² = 20 × 10⁻⁶ m² = 2.0 × 10⁻⁵ m²; L = 10 m; e = 2.5 cm = 0.025 m.

(A) Tensile stress = F/A = 200/(2.0 × 10⁻⁵) = 1.0 × 10⁷ N m⁻².
(B) Tensile strain = e/L = 0.025/10 = 2.5 × 10⁻³ (no unit).
(C) Young modulus = stress/strain = 1.0 × 10⁷/2.5 × 10⁻³ = 4.0 × 10⁹ N m⁻².

(iii) ΔV = 200 − 100 = 100 cm³ = 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ m³; p = 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa (constant).

Work done by the gas: W = pΔV = 1.0 × 10⁵ × 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ = 10 J.
Change in internal energy: ΔU = 1.5pΔV (p constant) = 1.5 × 10 = 15 J.

First law: Q = ΔU + W = 15 + 10 = 25 J.
The gas absorbs 25 J of heat.

subject: Physics
question:
a(i). State any three differences and one similarity each of standing and travelling waves.
(ii).Two travelling waves of equal amplitudes and equal frequencies move in opposite directions along a string. They interfere to produce standing waves having the equation:
y₁ = A sin(ωt − kx) and y₂ = A sin(ωt + kx) .
(A). Find the resultant when these waves superposed.
(B) What is the nature of amplitude of the resultant wave?
(C) Find the smallest points for node and antinode to be formed of the resultant wave.
modelAnswer:
(i) Differences:
1. A travelling wave transfers energy from one place to another; a standing wave does not transfer energy (the energy stays between the nodes).
2. In a travelling wave every particle vibrates with the same amplitude; in a standing wave the amplitude varies with position, from zero at nodes to a maximum at antinodes.
3. In a travelling wave neighbouring particles have different phases; in a standing wave all particles between two adjacent nodes vibrate in phase.
(Also: a travelling wave has no nodes or antinodes, while a standing wave has fixed nodes and antinodes.)

Similarity: both have a frequency and wavelength, and the particles of the medium vibrate in simple harmonic motion.

(ii) Note: y₁ and y₂ are the equations of the two travelling waves, not of standing waves. Their superposition gives the standing wave.

(A) By the principle of superposition, y = y₁ + y₂ = A sin(ωt − kx) + A sin(ωt + kx).
Using sin P + sin Q = 2 sin((P + Q)/2) cos((P − Q)/2), with (P + Q)/2 = ωt and (P − Q)/2 = −kx (and cos(−kx) = cos kx):
y = 2A cos kx sin ωt.

(B) The amplitude of the resultant is 2A cos kx. It depends on position x and not on time: it varies from 0 (where cos kx = 0) to a maximum of 2A (where cos kx = ±1). This shows the wave is stationary.

(C) Nodes occur where the amplitude is zero: cos kx = 0, so kx = π/2, 3π/2, ...
x = (2n + 1)π/(2k) = (2n + 1)λ/4, n = 0, 1, 2, ...
Smallest node position: x = λ/4 (using k = 2π/λ).

Antinodes occur where the amplitude is maximum: cos kx = ±1, so kx = 0, π, 2π, ...
x = nλ/2, n = 0, 1, 2, ...
Smallest antinode position: x = 0 (the next is at x = λ/2).

subject: Physics
question:
b(i). White light is a mixture of light of wavelengths between the limits 400nm and 700nm, When white light passes through water, what are the limits of the wavelength? Refractive index of water is 1.33.
(ii) A steel wire of length 64 cm weighs 5 g. If it is stretched by a force of 8 N, what would be the speed of a transverse wave passing on it?
modelAnswer:
(i) When light enters a medium, its frequency is unchanged but its speed and wavelength are reduced by the refractive index: λ_water = λ_air/n.

Lower limit: 400/1.33 ≈ 301 nm.
Upper limit: 700/1.33 ≈ 526 nm.

In water, the wavelengths lie between about 301 nm and 526 nm.

(ii) Mass per unit length: μ = m/L = 0.005 kg/0.64 m = 7.8125 × 10⁻³ kg m⁻¹.

Speed of a transverse wave on a stretched string: v = √(T/μ).
v = √(8/7.8125 × 10⁻³) = √1024 = 32 m s⁻¹.

subject: Physics
question:
a(i). Define the following terms pitch, resonance and Doppler effect as applied to sound waves.
(ii)An ultrasound signal of frequency 50 kHz is sent vertically into sea water. The signal gets reflected from the ocean bed and returns to the surface 0.80 s after it was emitted. The speed of sound in sea water is 1500 ms⁻¹. Find the depth of the sea and the wavelength of this signal in water.
modelAnswer:
(i) Pitch: the characteristic of a sound that tells how high or low it is; it depends on the frequency of the sound (higher frequency means higher pitch).
Resonance: the large-amplitude vibration produced in a body when it is made to vibrate by a periodic force whose frequency equals its own natural frequency.
Doppler effect: the apparent change in the frequency (pitch) of a sound heard by an observer when there is relative motion between the source and the observer.

(ii) The signal travels down to the sea bed and back, so the time for one way is 0.80/2 = 0.40 s.

Depth: d = v × t = 1500 × 0.40 = 600 m.

Wavelength: λ = v/f = 1500/(50 × 10³) = 0.030 m (3.0 cm).

subject: Physics
question:
b(i). Two trains move towards each other at a speed of 90 kmh⁻¹ relative to the earth's surface. One gives a 520 Hz signal. Find the frequency heard by the observer on the other train. The speed of sound wave in air is 350ms⁻¹.
(ii) On a winter day, sound travels 336 meters in one second. Find the atmospheric temperature in °C. Speed of sound at 0°C = 332 ms⁻¹.
modelAnswer:
(i) Note: this question gives the speed of sound as 350 m s⁻¹, not the 340 m s⁻¹ in the list of constants, so 350 m s⁻¹ is used.

Each train's speed: 90 km h⁻¹ = 90 × 1000/3600 = 25 m s⁻¹.
Source and observer move towards each other:
f' = f(v + u_o)/(v − u_s)
= 520 × (350 + 25)/(350 − 25)
= 520 × 375/325
= 600 Hz.

(ii) Speed of sound in air is proportional to the square root of the absolute temperature: v ∝ √T.
v/v₀ = √(T/T₀), so T = T₀(v/v₀)².

v = 336 m s⁻¹, v₀ = 332 m s⁻¹, T₀ = 273 K.
T = 273 × (336/332)² = 273 × (1.01205)² = 273 × 1.02424 ≈ 279.6 K.

Temperature = 279.6 − 273 ≈ 6.6°C.
